bibl.title: A model of subjective report and objective discrimination as categorical decisions in a vast representational space

span.label: why a stimulus can be discriminated above chance while being reported as unseen, treated as two decisions over the same sensory vector under different sets of response classes
span.quote: We show how a minimalist framework based on Signal Detection Theory and Bayesian inference can account for this dissociation, by describing subjective and objective tasks with similar decision-theoretic mechanisms. Each of these tasks relies on distinct response classes, and therefore distinct priors and decision boundaries. As a result, they may reach different conclusions.

span.label: whether objective and subjective tasks can be described by the same inference principles, differing only in the nature and size of the decision space
span.quote: Here, building upon earlier proposals [ 8 , 12 ], we explore a simple theoretical idea: objective and subjective tasks rely on the same inference principles, but they differ in the nature and size of the decision space.

span.label: a geometric decision model that reproduces six standard findings in conscious and unconscious perception without postulating a separate conscious process, and a new experiment confirming one of its predictions
span.quote: Furthermore, the model provides a set of original predictions on the nonlinear profiles of discrimination performance obtained at various levels of visibility. We successfully test one such prediction in a novel experiment: when varying continuously the degree of perceptual ambiguity between two visual symbols presented at perceptual threshold, identification performance varies quasi-linearly when the stimulus is unseen and in an ‘all-or-none’ manner when it is seen.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: We show how a minimalist framework based on Signal Detection Theory and Bayesian inference can account for this dissociation, by describing subjective and objective tasks with similar decision-theoretic mechanisms.

span.label: dissociation between subjective visibility report and objective discrimination (subliminal perception)
span.quote: Subliminal perception studies have shown that one can objectively discriminate a stimulus without subjectively perceiving it.

span.label: simulation
span.quote: In the following simulations, we use a series of computational simplifications.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Objective and subjective tasks apply the same maximum-a-posteriori inference to the same input vector, but over different response classes; the different class sets carry different priors and hence different decision boundaries, so the two tasks can return conflicting answers.
span.quote: Each of these tasks relies on distinct response classes, and therefore distinct priors and decision boundaries.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Internal noise makes some threshold trials yield shorter input vectors; short vectors both fall in the 'absent' region and sit nearer the X/Y discrimination boundary, so trials called unseen are automatically the ones discriminated worse.
span.quote: As a consequence of this variability, sensory inputs reported as unseen are associated with a shorter input vector and are therefore closer to the X / Y discrimination border than samples reported as seen

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Evidence weak enough to be classified as unseen necessarily lies near the origin of the representational space, where the forced-choice psychometric curve is shallow, producing linear (rather than all-or-none) unconscious response profiles.
span.quote: According to the present model, the reason why unconscious responses tend to be linearly related to stimulus evidence is simple: when perceptual evidence is low enough to be categorized as unseen, the evidence necessarily lies close to the origin of the multi-dimensional space and therefore leads to shallow (though above-chance) forced-choice curves.

span.label: each task imposes its own set of response classes on the same continuous vector space, so two tasks can partition it differently and return different answers
span.quote: Our third assumption is that each behavioural task imposes, in a top-down manner, a categorical structure of classes to this continuous vector space (e.g. ‘click left for faces and right for non-faces’). Performing the task consists in identifying, on every trial, the class in which the input vector falls. Formally, this is a statistical inference problem: in order to perform optimally, given a sensory input and prior knowledge, subjects should attempt to compute the posterior probability of each of the classes in order to select the class with the maximum a posteriori (MAP) choice, which is the one most likely to be correct. Each task imposes distinct, possibly overlapping response classes, and may therefore lead to different answers.

span.label: the distance between the two stimulus classes can exceed their distance from the absent class, which is why discrimination survives where detection does not
span.quote: The geometry of the two-dimensional model reveals why discrimination performance (i.e. d’ of X / Y discrimination) can be higher than detection sensitivity (i.e. d’ of absent/not-absent judgement): the distance separating the X and Y vectors is larger than that separating them from the absent class. In the two-dimensional case, discrimination performance is √2 higher than detection performance ( figure 2 a ). Consequently, given adequate statistical power, discrimination may be significantly above chance when detection sensitivity is not.

span.label: internal variability alone makes half of physically identical threshold stimuli fall nearer the absent class and be reported unseen, and those samples sit closer to the discrimination border
span.note: status: the paper's own words: can explain why
span.quote: Even when the stimuli are physically identical, internal variability can explain why approximately 50% of them are reported as unseen (those which are most similar to the absent class). As a consequence of this variability, sensory inputs reported as unseen are associated with a shorter input vector and are therefore closer to the X / Y discrimination border than samples reported as seen ( figure 2 b ). The simple hypothesis of a noisy input vector, together with non-orthogonal discrimination and detection tasks, suffices to explain why unseen trials generally exhibit a lower discrimination performance than seen trials.

span.label: the variance of the representation is what turns the visibility sigmoid from stepwise to nearly linear
span.quote: Interestingly, although the fraction of seen responses is always a sigmoid, its slope may vary from a stepwise ‘all-or-none’ pattern to a shallow and near-linear function. The parameter driving this change in sigmoid slope is the variance in representational space.

span.label: raising the prior for one stimulus lowers the visibility threshold for that stimulus alone, which is offered as the mechanism behind hysteresis effects
span.quote: Similarly, Melloni et al. [ 29 ] recently used a hysteresis paradigm in which letters were embedded in white noise. Across a series of trials, the identity of the letter was fixed while its signal-to-noise ratio gradually increased and then gradually decreased. Subjects reported seeing the letter better in the descending than in the ascending condition (i.e. once they knew the identity of the letter), even for identical physical stimulation.

span.label: if attention changes the variance of the input, it can raise or lower visibility depending on how many trials are already reported unseen
span.quote: Importantly, however, if P (absent) is high, so that most trials are reported as unseen, then increasing the stimulus variance still diminishes discrimination performance, but may paradoxically increase visibility ratings. This is because with higher variance, a greater number of samples fall outside the region responded as unseen and thus become subjectively visible ( figure 4 c ). The model therefore predicts that attention can induce opposite effects on visibility and discrimination performance even when the mean evidence is unchanged.

span.label: The account of linear versus nonlinear visibility profiles rests on an internal-variance parameter that cannot be measured in existing experiments.
span.quote: Because there is no unequivocal way of determining the internal variance of sensory inputs in existing experiments, the present account remains speculative.

span.label: The model assumes a decision based on one static input vector rather than an accumulation of samples over time.
span.quote: Another limit of the present model lies in its assumption, shared with SDT, that decisions are based on a single input vector.

span.label: Most of the model's coverage of the literature is post hoc rather than predictive.
span.quote: Most the above arguments account for empirical observations only in retrospect.

span.label: most of the account is retrospective, which is why a new experiment was run
span.quote: Most the above arguments account for empirical observations only in retrospect. We thus opted to confront the present model to a novel experimental set-up.

span.label: the internal variance that drives the central prediction cannot be determined from existing experiments, so that part of the account remains speculative
span.quote: Because there is no unequivocal way of determining the internal variance of sensory inputs in existing experiments, the present account remains speculative. Nevertheless, stimulus variance could be explicitly manipulated in future experiments.

span.label: six computational simplifications are declared in order: the cost function neglected, priors fixed in a given context rather than continuously updated, Gaussian distributions assumed, subjects assumed to have an accurate estimate of stimulus distributions, the same input vector entering different tasks, and stimulus evidence treated as a single discrete point
span.quote: In the following simulations, we use a series of computational simplifications. First, we neglect the cost function associated with each decision—sometimes referred to as ‘loss’ or ‘utility’ function. In the presence of costs, the optimal decision is the one which minimizes the expected loss and may differ from the MAP. Mathematically, however, priors and costs play a similar role and were thus merged in the present paper for simplicity. Second, the present model assumes that priors are fixed in a given context, rather than continuously updated after each decision. Assuming modifiable priors would lead to important new predictions, but would also increase the number of ad-hoc parameters in the models (e.g. learning rate, estimated world volatility, creation or deletion of classes). Third, we assume Gaussian distributions in order to facilitate the computations. Fourth, importantly, we assume that subjects have an accurate estimate of stimulus distributions—although following Lau [ 12 , 35 ], we will discuss the important consequences that ensue when subjects’ priors and likelihood functions are inappropriately calibrated. Fifth, we assume that, on a given trial, the same input vector enters into different tasks, thus neglecting the possibility that the internal evidence evoked by a fixed stimulus may vary with the task, owing, for instance, to decay [ 15 , 36 ], noise level [ 25 ], attention [ 37 ] or other top-down changes. Finally, we treat stimulus evidence on a given trial as a single discrete point in the n -dimensional space.

span.label: the hypothesis that the input vector remains unchanged and identically available for a series of successive judgements may turn out to be simplistic, given temporal decay, an attentional cue presented after the stimulus, the task set imposed by the first task, and the order in which two questions are presented
span.quote: Nevertheless, in other contexts, the hypothesis that the input vector remains unchanged and identically available for a series of successive judgements may turn out to be simplistic. Temporal decay may affect the quality of decisions made after a delay [ 66 ], particularly for unconscious stimuli [ 15 , 36 ]. A recent study suggests that an attentional cue presented after a sensory stimulus can retroactively improve its visibility [ 37 ]. The task set imposed by the first task may also change the quality of the evidence available for the second task [ 67 ]. Similarly, the order in which two questions are presented may influence the subject's answers

span.label: the model assumes a single input vector where sequential sampling models assume an accumulation, and extending it that way would be needed to predict reaction times
span.quote: Another limit of the present model lies in its assumption, shared with SDT, that decisions are based on a single input vector. A natural extension of the model would represent a sensory input as a series of samples, i.e. a trajectory in multi-dimensional space. Indeed, SDT has been superseded by sequential sampling models [ 70 – 72 ], according to which each decision is based on an accumulation of noisy samples arising from the stimulus. Whichever accumulator first reaches a fixed threshold is selected as the winner of the perceptual decision.

span.label: the assumption that the decision system is fully informed of the stimulus distributions is called undoubtedly an idealization, with a dynamic model whose likelihood functions, priors and costs are learned and may therefore be ill estimated offered as the route to human deviations from optimality
span.quote: In the tradition of ‘ideal observer’ analyses, we also assumed that the decision system is fully informed of the stimulus distributions and uses optimal priors and likelihood functions to compute the posterior probability of each response class. This is undoubtedly an idealization. A dynamic model in which the likelihood functions, priors and costs would be learned by updating them after each trial, and may therefore be ill estimated, may go a long way towards explaining a variety of human deviations from optimality.

span.label: the predicted exceptions to the all-or-none pattern, at high variance or low signal to noise, remain untested
span.quote: The present model readily reproduces this nonlinear pattern ( figure 4 a ) but it also predicts exceptions in cases of high stimulus variance or low signal-to-noise ratio. These predictions remain untested, but may offer potential explanations to studies revealing a continuous relationship between stimulus evidence and subjective reports [ 27 , 41 , 45 , 46 ]. In the future, directly manipulating the mean and the variance of stimulus evidence could clarify the role of each of these factors in linear and nonlinear response patterns to sensory manipulations.

span.label: the MAP rule, which supplies the decision boundaries instead of their being assumed
span.quote: This MAP criterion results in the segregation of representational space into distinct regions separated by sharp decision boundaries (importantly, the placement of these boundaries does not constitute an additional hypothesis of the model, but derives directly from the hypothesis that decisions are based on a MAP criterion).

span.label: likelihood distributions and a decision rule, moved from one axis into a multi-dimensional space
span.quote: Indeed, although SDT is not limited to a single dimension, it is often depicted as a binary problem with two Gaussian distributions plotted along a single axis. We argue that this classic diagram fails to capture the interaction between multiple features, classes and tasks, whereas a two-dimensional depiction fulfils these requirements

span.label: non-commuting projections, offered as a way to model why the order of two questions changes the answers
span.quote: Busemeyer et al. [ 69 ] have proposed accounting for the latter phenomenon with a computational principle inspired from quantum mechanics, according to which each successive judgement alters the input vector by projecting it onto a subspace defined by the task. As projections are not commutative, the order of successive questions can change the successive decisions. It remains to be seen whether such non-commutativity is a fundamental principle that should be added to the present model.

span.label: within-category compression and between-category separation as the definition to be met
span.quote: According to Harnad's definition [ 53 ], categorical perception is defined by ‘within-category compression and between-category separation’. In a companion paper in preparation, we will present additional evidence that the conscious experience of our morphs follows Harnad's definition of categorical perception [ 53 ]. First, discriminability is indeed enhanced for pairs of digits presented near the perceptual boundary. Second, when presented with two identical ambiguous morphs, subjects frequently judge that the stimuli differ, as predicted if each has an approximately 50% chance of falling in either of two discrete perceptual categories. Third, when the present identification task is replicated using a continuous response scale, subjects respond bimodally and barely use the intermediate levels to report perceiving a mixture of two digits.

span.label: two subjects excluded for failing to converge to a stable threshold
span.note: eliminates: a threshold estimate that never settled, which would put an unmeasurable visibility level into the group analysis
span.quote: Two subjects who failed to converge to a stable threshold were excluded.

span.label: discrimination → visibility
span.note: A DEPENDENCE, AND A SAMENESS CLAIM UNDERNEATH IT: the model predicts that linear and nonlinear response profiles ARISE FROM THE SAME DECISION MECHANISM, and that the discrimination profile of physically identical stimuli becomes increasingly nonlinear AS VISIBILITY INCREASES. No type expresses 'these vary together because one mechanism produces both'.
span.quote: The model critically predicts that linear and nonlinear profiles of behavioural responses arise from the same decision mechanism . In particular, it predicts that the discrimination profile of physically identical stimuli will increasingly become nonlinear as visibility increases

span.label: THE SAME INPUT UNDER TWO CLASS STRUCTURES GIVES TWO ANSWERS, AND BOTH ARE CORRECT: each task imposes, top-down, its own categorical structure on one continuous space, and distinct response classes may therefore lead to different conclusions
span.quote: Our third assumption is that each behavioural task imposes, in a top-down manner, a categorical structure of classes to this continuous vector space (e.g. ‘click left for faces and right for non-faces’). Performing the task consists in identifying, on every trial, the class in which the input vector falls. Formally, this is a statistical inference problem: in order to perform optimally, given a sensory input and prior knowledge, subjects should attempt to compute the posterior probability of each of the classes in order to select the class with the maximum a posteriori (MAP) choice, which is the one most likely to be correct. Each task imposes distinct, possibly overlapping response classes, and may therefore lead to different answers.

span.label: so a dissociation between what is discriminated and what is reported needs no second process - it is what one inference looks like when the question changes
span.quote: These results confirm that, for physically identical stimuli, visibility is associated with a greater degree of ‘all-or-none’ perception, a finding that the framework can explain without any additional assumption (i.e. no need to postulate a qualitative difference between conscious and unconscious processing).

span.label: THE BOUNDARIES ARE DERIVED, NOT POSITED: their placement is stated not to be an additional hypothesis but a consequence of choosing the most probable class
span.quote: This MAP criterion results in the segregation of representational space into distinct regions separated by sharp decision boundaries (importantly, the placement of these boundaries does not constitute an additional hypothesis of the model, but derives directly from the hypothesis that decisions are based on a MAP criterion).

span.label: A WIDELY USED TERM WHOSE ORDINARY FORM IS WRONG: criterion suggests a single scalar value, and in this framework it is a set of task-specific boundaries dividing a space, which move when the task or the priors move
span.quote: This account formalizes the hypothesis that blindsight patients have an inappropriate ‘criterion’ for visibility judgement (e.g. [ 12 , 35 , 43 ]). Note, however, that the concept of criterion can be misleading because it incorrectly suggests a single scalar value. In the present framework, the ‘criterion’ emerges as a set of decisional boundaries that delimit the categorical regions in the representational space, and that are specific to the selected task. A change in the task or in the priors may thus impose a different division of space, and hence a shift in decision boundaries;

span.label: THE BIAS IS THE SIGNAL: a shift in visibility criterion reflects the subject's own priors and costs and is argued not to be an experimental confound to be discarded
span.quote: In the present model, subjective visibility reports reflect a legitimate decision process whose details (including response bias) can and should be accounted for. As recently demonstrated [ 29 , 30 , 61 ], a shift in visibility criterion reflects the underlying prior probabilities and cost functions of the subjects’ internal model of the world, and, consequently, should not be disregarded as an experimental confound. What we call a ‘subjective’ report may simply be the brain's best attempt at solving a difficult perceptual decision problem with myriads of potential classes, each with different costs and prior probabilities that depend on the subject's prior experience.

span.label: THE CONTROL CREATES THE CONFOUND IT WAS MEANT TO REMOVE: equating discrimination by masking or by attention introduces physical differences between the visible and invisible stimuli, so the contrast may reflect the stimulus rather than the visibility
span.quote: The present geometrical analysis suggests that Lau's experiments have adopted only a subset of the possible solutions: both masking the stimuli at different levels [ 24 ] and changing the amount of attention they receive [ 26 ] may change the signal-to-noise ratio of the incoming evidence. However, under such conditions, discrimination performance is equated at the expense of introducing physical differences between the visible and invisible stimuli. It is therefore unclear whether contrasting the two reflects an effect of visibility or of the stimulus’ physical properties. Consequently, it may be preferable to use physically identical stimuli and alter subjective visibility by changing the priors ( figure 3 a )—a solution indeed adopted in several recent studies

span.label: AND THE PAPER SAYS ITS OWN ARGUMENTS ARE RETROSPECTIVE before running a new experiment - the accommodation of six existing findings is not offered as the test
span.quote: Most the above arguments account for empirical observations only in retrospect. We thus opted to confront the present model to a novel experimental set-up.

span.label: the target set is declared first: six empirical findings that any account should reproduce, listed before the model is built
span.quote: Specifically, we identified six major sets of empirical findings that should be accounted for: — Stimuli which are subjectively reported as ‘unseen’ can nevertheless be objectively discriminated above chance in a two-alternative forced-choice task [ 9 , 16 , 19 – 22 ]. — Discrimination performance is typically better on seen than on unseen trials, even when sensory stimuli are physically identical [ 23 – 25 ]. — Experimental paradigms can be designed in which objective discrimination performance is identical, while subjective visibility differs [ 12 , 24 , 26 ]. — Subjective reports vary nonlinearly as a function of sensory strength. For instance, brief or faint visual stimuli are generally reported as ‘completely unseen’, but once their duration or contrast reaches a threshold level, subjects tend to report items as ‘clearly seen’ [ 23 , 25 , 27 – 29 ]. — Prior knowledge increases the subjective visibility of physically identical stimuli [ 29 – 32 ]. — Attention generally increases subjective visibility but has also been found to decrease it

span.label: AND THE ORDER OF THE QUESTIONS MAY CHANGE THE ANSWERS: successive judgements may project the vector onto a task-defined subspace, and projections do not commute
span.quote: Busemeyer et al. [ 69 ] have proposed accounting for the latter phenomenon with a computational principle inspired from quantum mechanics, according to which each successive judgement alters the input vector by projecting it onto a subspace defined by the task. As projections are not commutative, the order of successive questions can change the successive decisions. It remains to be seen whether such non-commutativity is a fundamental principle that should be added to the present model.

span.label: an explanation is removed rather than added: a linear-then-categorical pattern previously read as two processes is reproduced by one, with the extra kind declared unnecessary
span.quote: Our results extend a previous study by de Gardelle et al. [ 47 ], which examined the amount of masked repetition priming elicited by a morphed face when the prime was unmasked (SOA = 300 ms) or heavily masked stimuli (SOA = 43 ms). As in the present experiment, they observed linearly increasing priming for invisible morphs and categorical priming for visible morphs. Although the authors proposed that this dissociation reflected two distinct processes (unconscious analogue versus conscious discrete), the present model suggests that this interpretation is unnecessary: even within a single decision process, response patterns may vary in their degree of nonlinearity depending on the mean and variance of the stimulus evidence.

span.label: claim_type: mechanism
span.note: a second reading reaching the same value. Recorded: mechanism — a second reading reaching the same value from a different sentence. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: The present model highlights how conscious and non-conscious decisions may correspond to distinct categorizations of the same stimulus encoded by a high-dimensional neuronal population vector.

span.label: method: a Bayesian signal-detection model in a multi-dimensional feature space, simulated for six known findings, then tested behaviourally by morphing one bar between two digits at perceptual threshold and collecting identification and visibility on every trial
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: simulation — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: We tested this prediction by linearly varying a parameter λ to create a continuum between two perceptual classes X and Y ( figure 5 ). For λ = 0, the stimulus is X , for λ = 1, the stimulus is Y , but we can create an arbitrary series of intermediate stimuli S ( λ ) = λX + (1 – λ ) Y . Whereas de Gardelle et al. [ 47 ] used a linear morph between two faces, here we varied the contrast of a single line to create a continuum between two different digits

span.label: phenomenon: subliminal perception: above-chance discrimination of a stimulus the subject reports not having seen
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: dissociation between subjective visibility report and objective discrimination (subliminal perception) — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: This finding could be trivial if the visibility judgement was systematically biased towards the unseen response (and indeed such response bias has often been proposed as an interpretation of subliminal perception experiments [ 42 ]). However, our simulations assume a Bayes-optimal inference process. Thus, we show that there are conditions under which the absent or unseen response is the most probable one, and yet X versus Y can still be discriminated.

span.label: builds-on → earlier proposals [8, 12] (including Lau's decision-theoretic account)
span.quote: Here, building upon earlier proposals [ 8 , 12 ], we explore a simple theoretical idea: objective and subjective tasks rely on the same inference principles, but they differ in the nature and size of the decision space.

span.label: extends → de Gardelle et al. [47]
span.quote: Our results extend a previous study by de Gardelle et al. [ 47 ], which examined the amount of masked repetition priming elicited by a morphed face when the prime was unmasked (SOA = 300 ms) or heavily masked stimuli (SOA = 43 ms).

span.label: contradicts → Rahnev et al. [26]
span.note: differs in: what drives the visibility rating: Rahnev has attention inducing a bias BY CHANGING THE INTER-TRIAL VARIANCE OF THE STIMULUS, where this model predicts AN INTERACTION BETWEEN THE VARIANCE AND INITIAL VISIBILITY THRESHOLD
span.quote: Contrary to Rahnev et al. [ 26 ], who argue that attention induces a conservative visibility bias by changing the inter-trial variance of the stimulus, we predict that visibility ratings are influenced by an interaction between the variance and initial visibility threshold (determined by prior knowledge or stimulus evidence).

span.label: critiques → accounts on which conscious perception is qualitatively different - more integrated, or dependent on higher-order metacognitive representations
span.note: differs in: quantitative against qualitative: CONSCIOUS PROCESSES ARE QUANTITATIVELY MORE COMPLEX, INTEGRATED AND DIFFERENTIATED (Tononi and Edelman) against CONSCIOUS PERCEPTION IS QUALITATIVELY DIFFERENT FROM UNCONSCIOUS PERCEPTION, AS IT RELIES ON HIGHER ORDER METACOGNITIVE REPRESENTATIONS (Lau, Rosenthal)
span.quote: For instance, Tononi & Edelman [ 11 ] have argued that conscious processes are quantitatively more complex, integrated and differentiated than unconscious processes. Lau [ 12 ] and Rosenthal [ 13 ] claim that conscious perception is qualitatively different from unconscious perception, as it relies on higher order metacognitive representations. Recent empirical studies challenge these accounts, however. First, subliminal stimuli can recruit complex semantic and integrative processes [ 14 – 16 ]. Second, even second-order metacognitive inferences can apparently be performed above chance on unseen stimuli

span.label: explains-away → the reading of linear unconscious and categorical conscious priming as two distinct processes
span.quote: Our results extend a previous study by de Gardelle et al. [ 47 ], which examined the amount of masked repetition priming elicited by a morphed face when the prime was unmasked (SOA = 300 ms) or heavily masked stimuli (SOA = 43 ms). As in the present experiment, they observed linearly increasing priming for invisible morphs and categorical priming for visible morphs. Although the authors proposed that this dissociation reflected two distinct processes (unconscious analogue versus conscious discrete), the present model suggests that this interpretation is unnecessary: even within a single decision process, response patterns may vary in their degree of nonlinearity depending on the mean and variance of the stimulus evidence.

span.label: critiques → the methodological position that subjective reports are unreliable and objective sensitivity measures should be preferred
span.note: differs in: whether one measure reduces to the other: WE SHOW THAT SUBJECTIVE REPORTS CANNOT BE REDUCED TO OBJECTIVE MEASURES, against the position that OBJECTIVE MEASURES, FOR EXAMPLE DETECTION SENSITIVITY (d'), SHOULD BE FAVOURED
span.quote: Firstly, the present model goes against the idea that subjective reports of ‘not seeing’ are necessarily unreliable because they can be affected by conservative response biases [ 33 , 42 , 59 , 60 ] and that objective measures, for example detection sensitivity ( d’ ), should be favoured (see review in [ 16 ]). On the contrary, we show that subjective reports cannot be reduced to objective measures [ 42 , 59 , 60 ] nor to the second-order measures such as confidence rating and post-decision wagering

span.label: qualifies → Lau and colleagues' designs that equate discrimination across seen and unseen trials, which do so at the cost of physical stimulus differences
span.note: differs in: what the design holds constant and what it lets vary: DISCRIMINATION PERFORMANCE IS EQUATED AT THE EXPENSE OF INTRODUCING PHYSICAL DIFFERENCES between the conditions, since masking and attention BOTH MAY CHANGE THE SIGNAL-TO-NOISE RATIO OF THE INCOMING EVIDENCE
span.quote: The present geometrical analysis suggests that Lau's experiments have adopted only a subset of the possible solutions: both masking the stimuli at different levels [ 24 ] and changing the amount of attention they receive [ 26 ] may change the signal-to-noise ratio of the incoming evidence. However, under such conditions, discrimination performance is equated at the expense of introducing physical differences between the visible and invisible stimuli. It is therefore unclear whether contrasting the two reflects an effect of visibility or of the stimulus’ physical properties. Consequently, it may be preferable to use physically identical stimuli and alter subjective visibility by changing the priors ( figure 3 a )—a solution indeed adopted in several recent studies

span.label: contradicts → Rahnev and colleagues' account of attention as inducing a conservative visibility bias through inter-trial variance
span.note: differs in: the same parameter as item 2: variance alone against AN INTERACTION BETWEEN THE VARIANCE AND INITIAL VISIBILITY THRESHOLD
span.quote: Contrary to Rahnev et al. [ 26 ], who argue that attention induces a conservative visibility bias by changing the inter-trial variance of the stimulus, we predict that visibility ratings are influenced by an interaction between the variance and initial visibility threshold

span.quote: Indeed, although SDT is not limited to a single dimension, it is often depicted as a binary problem with two Gaussian distributions plotted along a single axis. We argue that this classic diagram fails to capture the interaction between multiple features, classes and tasks, whereas a two-dimensional depiction fulfils these requirements

span.label: extends → de Gardelle and colleagues' morphed-face priming result, replicated here with digits and an explicit visibility scale
span.quote: Our results extend a previous study by de Gardelle et al. [ 47 ], which examined the amount of masked repetition priming elicited by a morphed face when the prime was unmasked (SOA = 300 ms) or heavily masked stimuli (SOA = 43 ms). As in the present experiment, they observed linearly increasing priming for invisible morphs and categorical priming for visible morphs. Although the authors proposed that this dissociation reflected two distinct processes (unconscious analogue versus conscious discrete), the present model suggests that this interpretation is unnecessary: even within a single decision process, response patterns may vary in their degree of nonlinearity depending on the mean and variance of the stimulus evidence.

span.label: task —causes→ classes
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — THE WHOLE ARGUMENT: each task imposes, top-down, its own categorical structure on a continuous space, and distinct response classes may therefore lead to different answers about the same input
span.quote: Our third assumption is that each behavioural task imposes, in a top-down manner, a categorical structure of classes to this continuous vector space (e.g. ‘click left for faces and right for non-faces’). Performing the task consists in identifying, on every trial, the class in which the input vector falls. span.label: response classes —part-of→ task
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — and a confidence judgement is just another set of classes, so there is one confidence per task rather than one confidence
span.quote: For each of them, the second-order ‘confidence’ judgement can also be performed by setting additional response classes, corresponding to whether the first-order decision has a high or low probability of being correct. As shown graphically in figure 1 c , there is a distinct confidence judgement associated with each primary task. At the expense of Persaud et al. [ 38 ] and Lau et al. [ 12 ], we note that the second-order tasks need not coincide with visibility judgement.

span.label: decision boundaries —operationalised-as→ criterion
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — DERIVED, NOT POSITED: their placement is stated not to be an additional hypothesis but a consequence of choosing the most probable class
span.quote: This MAP criterion results in the segregation of representational space into distinct regions separated by sharp decision boundaries (importantly, the placement of these boundaries does not constitute an additional hypothesis of the model, but derives directly from the hypothesis that decisions are based on a MAP criterion).

span.label: criterion —part-of→ representational space
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — A TERM WHOSE ORDINARY FORM IS WRONG: criterion suggests a single scalar, and here it is a task-specific set of boundaries that move when the task or the priors move
span.quote: This account formalizes the hypothesis that blindsight patients have an inappropriate ‘criterion’ for visibility judgement (e.g. [ 12 , 35 , 43 ]).
